documents.abstract: Abstract The rapid development of digital technologies has transformed modern society in almost every sphere of human life. The growth of the internet, smartphones, social media, artificial intelligence, cloud computing, big data, digital payments, e-commerce, and online education has created what is commonly described as a digital society. Digital technologies have improved communication, access to information, education, healthcare, business, public administration, and economic participation. At the same time, the increasing dependence on digital systems has created significant ethical challenges relating to privacy, data protection, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, misinformation, digital inequality, online harassment, intellectual property, surveillance, and the responsible use of emerging technologies.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Natural disasters demand rapid synthesis of fragmented, heterogeneous data often distributed across independently governed organizations. This paper introduces DisasterAI, a federated, cloud-native, and multi-modal AI architecture for disaster intelligence. Unlike centralized analytics platforms, DisasterAI emphasizes federated data ingestion, modular adapters, and the alignment of derived intelligence—enabling cross-agency coordination without requiring raw data consolidation. The architecture integrates satellite imagery (optical and SAR), IoT sensor streams, public alerts, and contextual civic data into a unified, explainable decision-support pipeline. DisasterAI addresses critical challenges in disaster intelligence, including spatial-temporal alignment of asynchronous data, modality-aware fusion, uncertainty representation, and fairness-aware decision-making. Designed to support the entire disaster lifecycle—from early warning and forecast-informed risk analysis to impact assessment and response prioritization—it operates within a human-in-the-loop decision-support context. A scenario-driven evaluation illustrates how DisasterAI enhances coordination effectiveness, improves prioritization consistency, and maintains robustness under partial data availability. By focusing on architectural behavior and operational integration rather than algorithmic benchmarking, this work positions federated, explainable AI systems as a viable foundation for scalable and reliable disaster-response frameworks in complex, data-constrained environments.

Generative AI is rapidly reshaping STEM higher education. Not only are our educational practices changing, but how we think about educational transformation must also adapt. Existing models of institutional change in STEM, aimed at interactive engagement, have largely followed an adoption logic: relatively stable, well-researched educational practices are evaluated and then scaled. These assumptions do not hold for generative AI, which is an arrival technology – entering classrooms before a sufficient pedagogical evidence base could form, and requiring institutions to act under uncertainty. Building on recent decades of work on STEM education institutional change, we propose a framework identifying six dimensions along which prior models of change must be adapted in light of AI: three concerning the tools at the center of reform (the tool’s evidence base, rate of change, and scope), and three concerning the people involved in change (faculty, change agents, and students). For each dimension, we examine how AI-era assumptions differ from those underlying prior STEM education reforms and derive design implications, including: privileging humble and local inquiries; organizing reform around pedagogical approaches rather than specific tools; repositioning change agents as facilitators of collective inquiry; and engaging students as partners in reform. Collectively, the six dimensions and design implications constitute a framework for adapting change models to support institutions under conditions of genuine uncertainty. Finally, we illustrate how the framework may be applied through a brief case-study of a faculty workshop series carried out in a university physics department to support instructors adapting to this modern AI era.

Future fighter operations are expected to combine increasingly capable autonomy, collaborative aircraft, dense sensor information, and sustained physiological and cognitive demands. This Perspective proposes a pilot-wellness-informed ecological framework in which the pilot, a pilot-specific digital twin, an intelligent flight-management system, the aircraft, and external agents are treated as interdependent elements within a systems-of-systems framework. The framework does not replace situation awareness, distributed cognition, joint cognitive systems, adaptive automation, or human-autonomy teaming. Instead, it extends their unit of analysis by making the pilot’s dynamic physiological and neurocognitive state, longitudinal variability, and health-related constraints explicit system variables and design objectives. The pilot digital twin is defined narrowly as an individualized state-estimation and forecasting capability, whereas the intelligent flight-management system integrates pilot, platform, mission, and environmental information to provide explainable recommendations and, where authorized, bounded adaptive action. We identify testable propositions concerning individualized prediction, adaptive support, shared situation awareness, trust calibration, and governance. The framework is prospective and requires validation in simulation, training, and operationally representative environments. Its purpose is to organize research toward systems that protect pilot agency, sustain performance, and preserve long-term health while exploiting increasingly autonomous teammates.

Electronic learning (e-learning) or online learning in medical education has become increasingly prevalent, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic. However, poor student engagement and reduced motivation are among the critical challenges associated with online learning. The e-learning for Renal Applied Pharmacology (e-RAP) is a new technology-enhanced learning tool that includes a nephron image augmented with several Quick Response (QR) codes. It allows students to access relevant QR-linked educational materials prepared by the teachers. This quasi-experimental pilot study examined whether use of the e-RAP tool was associated with differences in cognitive performance, engagement, and motivation among 105 preclinical medical students at Universiti Sultan Zainal Abidin (UniSZA), Malaysia. Participants in the intervention group (Year 2, n = 45) used the e-RAP tool, while the control group (Year 1, n = 60) received conventional teaching. Cognitive performance, engagement, and motivation scores were measured using pre- and posttest multiple-choice questions (MCQ), the Burch Engagement Survey for Students, and the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire, respectively. Both groups demonstrated improvements in mean cognitive scores from pre- to post-test MCQ, with greater gains in the intervention group than in the control group. The intervention group was also associated with higher emotional and cognitive engagement (both in and out of class) and higher scores in several motivational domains, including intrinsic value, cognitive strategy use, and selfregulation. Although groups differed by academic year, baseline knowledge was comparable. Taken together, these preliminary findings suggest that e-RAP use may be associated with differences in cognitive performance, engagement, and motivation.

The evolving dynamics of security management have necessitated the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in predictive intelligence and military operations in Africa. This integration presents a paradigm of significant opportunities alongside profound challenges. Theoretically, AI promises to enhance situational awareness, enable results-oriented conflict management, and optimize operational efficiency across the continent. However, this study posits that its deployment is fraught with daunting ethical and practical impediments specific to the African context. This work interrogates the ethical imperatives of AI in predictive intelligence and military operations in Africa. To achieve its objectives—which include defining context-specific ethical principles, diagnosing implementation barriers, and proposing a practical framework—the study adopted a mixed-methods approach. This methodology relied on semi-structured interviews with military personnel, defence analysts, and AI ethics scholars, complemented by a historicist content analysis of secondary sources including policy documents, institutional reports, and academic literature. The findings reveal a strong consensus among stakeholders on the paramount importance of ethical principles such as accountability, transparency, fairness, and meaningful human oversight. However, the study identified that the realisation of these principles is severely constrained by critical obstacles, including a stark infrastructure and data deficit, a pervasive regulatory and policy vacuum, and pre-existing governance frailties. These contextual challenges amplify ethical risks, particularly algorithmic bias and accountability gaps, threatening to exacerbate social divisions and undermine human security. Consequently, the study concludes that ethically responsible AI use is not an automatic outcome but must be actively cultivated. It recommends, among other measures, the urgent development of a continent-wide regulatory framework by the African Union to harmonise standards and prevent misuse. The study argues that only through such deliberate, multi-faceted interventions—combining robust regulation, strategic investment in digital infrastructure, and international collaboration on equitable terms—can Africa harness the benefits of AI for security while safeguarding fundamental ethical imperatives.

Abstract Despite the increasing adoption of automated/autonomous guided vehicles (AGVs) in precision agriculture, existing human-machine interfaces (HMIs) remain function-centric, frequently neglecting the cognitive and user experience (UX) needs of non-technical operators. Consequently, current dashboards suffer from limited usability, high cognitive load, and reduced system transparency, increasing the risk of operator error. To address this gap within agricultural teleoperation interface design, this study presents a theory-driven HMI framework that systematically translates Endsley’s Situational Awareness (SA) theory (Perception, Comprehension, Projection) and ISO 9241 ergonomic principles into a structured three-panel AGV teleoperation interface. Unlike conventional function-oriented dashboards, the proposed framework organises interface components according to operator cognitive requirements to support information perception, comprehension, and projection during remote operation. A theory-driven agricultural teleoperation HMI framework was developed by translating cognitive and ergonomic principles into practical interface organization strategies. To formatively evaluate this SA-driven design architecture, we conducted a user-perception study with non-expert digitally literate participants (N = 20), evaluating three iterative HMI prototypes. The comparative results indicate that the SA-aligned layout received higher user ratings in perceived decision-support capability (SA3), cognitive workload reduction, and overall usability compared with baseline designs during formative evaluation. The study provides preliminary methodological guidance for agricultural teleoperation HMI design, while recognizing that objective operational validation with target agricultural users remains necessary.

documents.abstract: Introduction To explore the psychological mechanisms of persistence in adult instrumental learning, this study investigates the associations among different types of teacher feedback, self-efficacy, and intrinsic motivation, and examines the moderating role of learning stages. Methods Using a cross-sectional survey design, scale and open-ended text data were collected from 743 adult violin learners. A moderated mediation model was tested through multiple regression and the Bootstrap method, supplemented by thematic analysis to provide a qualitative context. Results Data analysis indicates: (1) Positive feedback and constructive feedback are significantly and positively associated with intrinsic motivation ( β = 0.207, p < 0.001; β = 0.342, p < 0.001), while negative feedback shows a significant negative association ( β = −0.318, p < 0.001); (2) Self-efficacy demonstrates a significant partial mediating association between the three types of feedback and intrinsic motivation, with indirect effect estimates of 0.103, 0.098, and −0.097, respectively (95% CIs all exclude 0); (3) The learning stage significantly moderates the conditional indirect effects: as the learning stage advances, the indirect association of positive feedback on intrinsic motivation via self-efficacy gradually weakens (index of moderated mediation = −0.045), whereas the indirect association of constructive feedback gradually strengthens (index of moderated mediation = 0.038). Open-ended texts echo these statistical paths at the micro-level. Discussion The study shows that there are heterogeneous and dynamic statistical connections between teacher feedback and adult intrinsic motivation, and self-efficacy is a key pathway to understanding this connection. In practice, the provision of instructional feedback content should match the learners’ experience stage.

Abstract The increasing deployment of AI agents in operations management, spanning production scheduling, predictive maintenance, supply chain management, and energy systems, is progressively shifting automated systems from decision support tools to autonomous decision-making entities. Despite this transition, existing frameworks do not adequately characterize how humans and AI agents interact in operational decision-making contexts. This paper proposes a taxonomy of human-AI interaction patterns in agent-based operations management, developed through a theory-driven approach based on decision theory, control systems, human factors, and explainable AI research. The taxonomy articulates the interaction space along five analytically separable dimensions: Decision Trigger, Execution Authority, Human Entry Point, Human Influence and Interpretive Access. It identifies seven interaction patterns organized into four macro-patterns ordered by increasing AI operational autonomy. Illustrative examples drawn from scientific literature demonstrate the discriminative capacity of the taxonomy across heterogeneous operations management domains and agent architectures. The taxonomy provides researchers with an analytical instrument to characterize and compare human-AI decision loop configurations, and practitioners with a design reference for deliberate and accountable interaction choices in operational AI deployments.

Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption is widely studied at the organizational level, yet much less is known about the specific algorithms organizations adopt and the reasons for these choices. This study investigates AI adoption among research-and-development (R&D) small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and start-ups in Turkiye through a proposed expert-driven, learning-domain-based taxonomy comprising 28 algorithms grouped into seven AI families. Survey data were collected from 36 organizations affiliated with the Istanbul Chamber of Commerce. Reliability and validity were established, and adoption was examined through descriptive statistics and non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney tests. At the algorithm level, Decision Trees, Neural Networks, Multilayer Perceptron, and Linear Regression were the most adopted, reflecting a preference for interpretable, structurally familiar methods, whereas Deep Q-Network, Policy Gradient, and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping were the least adopted. At the family level, Unsupervised Learning and Natural Language Processing ranked highest, while Reinforcement Learning and Autonomous Behavior recorded the lowest and most divergent adoption. Adoption also varied by sector—Financial/FinTech and Engineering/Defense showed the broadest portfolios and Healthcare and Commerce/e-Commerce the narrowest—with statistically significant cross-sector differences for Autonomous Behavior and Unsupervised Learning. Adoption range increased across organizational stages, peaking at post-incubation. The findings extend the Technology-Organization-Environment framework with diffusion of innovation and dynamic capability theory to the algorithm level and emphasize AI algorithms’ knowledge as a target for SMEs’ digital transformation.

documents.abstract: The swift evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is dramatically changing the landscape of education, especially when it comes to assessment. Traditional methods, which focus heavily on standardized tests and final evaluations, are falling short in capturing the complex cognitive, social, and digital skills that are essential in today’s world. This paper delves into the transformative power of AI in educational assessment and suggests a strategic framework for embracing digital change. By reviewing current literature, the study highlights AI-driven innovations like adaptive testing, automated grading, learning analytics, and competency-based assessment models. It also tackles important challenges such as ethical issues, algorithmic bias, data privacy, and maintaining academic integrity. The paper emphasizes that a comprehensive, policy-oriented, and pedagogically sound approach are crucial for effectively integrating AI into assessment systems. In the end, it offers practical strategies for institutions aiming to update their assessment practices in an AI-enhanced educational environment.

Primary education represents the foundational stage of formal education, where children develop essential academic, cognitive, social, emotional, creative, and communication skills. The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into primary education offers new possibilities for personalized learning, interactive instruction, educational games, language development, accessibility, formative assessment, and teacher support. However, the use of AI at the primary level requires particular care because young learners may have limited ability to understand technological risks, evaluate AI-generated information, or protect their personal information independently. Therefore, AI should be introduced in an age-appropriate, safe, inclusive, and teacher-guided manner. The fundamental principle of AI in primary education is: Child → Teacher Guidance → AI-Supported Learning → Interaction → Feedback → Learning AI should support the educational process rather than replace teachers, parents, classroom interaction, play, creativity, or children's independent thinking.Artificial Intelligence in primary education refers to the use of AI-enabled technologies to support teaching, learning, assessment, educational communication, and the overall development of young learners. AI applications can provide personalized learning activities, interactive exercises, intelligent tutoring, language support, educational games, automated feedback, and assistive learning facilities. Examples of AI applications in primary education include intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, educational chatbots, speech-recognition applications, AI-supported language-learning systems, educational games, automated feedback tools, and AI-assisted teaching resources. The main purpose of AI at this level is to enhance the learning experience while keeping the teacher and the learner at the centre of education.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The increasing complexity, volatility, and sustainability pressures affecting global supply chains have accelerated the adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies in logistics management. Among these AI approaches, Intelligent Agents (IAs) and Multi-agent Systems (MAS) have emerged as essential tools for supporting decentralized, adaptive, event-driven, and real-time decision-making processes in dynamic logistics environments. Unlike traditional centralized planning systems, agent-based approaches enable autonomous entities such as suppliers, warehouses, transportation units, and distribution centers to coordinate actions, exchange information, and manage variability. This paper presents a structured literature review of peer-reviewed studies indexed in Scopus and Web of Science on the use of AI agents to support decision-making in logistics management and supply chain operations. Particular attention is given to the strategic importance of intelligent agents in strengthening resilience, operational efficiency, and sustainability in increasingly uncertain logistics systems. The findings indicate that intelligent agents improve decision quality, responsiveness, coordination, and resource utilization across distributed logistics networks. Furthermore, Multi-Agent Systems enhance interoperability and collaboration among logistics actors, enabling more agile and resilient supply chains. However, challenges related to data quality, cybersecurity, governance, scalability, and human–AI collaboration continue to limit large-scale implementation in industrial environments.
topics: Supply Chain Resilience and Risk Management

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is getting integrated into the day-to-day life of every human being. This fast-changing technology is transforming traditional technology, society and governance at a rapid pace. This paper explores the emerging Technorapid Age, where technological change may move faster than the ability of individuals, institutions and governance systems to adapt. It focuses on Responsible Innovation as a methodology to manage this growing gap. It proposes that AI development should not be measured only by technological progress. It should also consider human well-being, social inclusion, ethical responsibility and effective governance. It examines the relationship between AI, technology and society. It highlights the need for human adaptability, accountability and responsible decision-making. The author proposes that Responsible Innovation can help create an equilibrium between technological acceleration and human adaptive capacity. The paper directly connects with the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. India needs technological development that is innovative, inclusive, ethical and sustainable. Technology should support human dignity, social well-being and the needs of future generations. The research concludes that achieving Viksit Bharat 2047 requires comprehensive and responsible AI technologies. These innovations should benefit all sections of society (सर्वजन हिताय, सर्वजन सुखाय) and ensure that people are skilled and supported to handle challenges of the Technorapid Age.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming a major driver of India's digital transformation. It is expected to impact governance, education, healthcare, finance, employment and everyday life as India moves towards the vision of Viksit Bharat@2047. However, this rapid development and adoption of technology also creates a growing gap between technological progress and the ability of individuals and society to adapt. This paper describes this condition as Technorapid, an accelerating pace of technological change that can exceed human, social, institutional and ethical adaptive capacity. The paper proposes that digital transformation should not remain confined to policies and institutional documents. Its success should ultimately be visible on the ground, in the lived experience of its citizens. AI-driven development needs to be evaluated through its ability to improve access, dignity, inclusion, education, employment and quality of life. This paper explores Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, the principle that the world is one family, as a philosophical foundation for a human-centered approach to AI ethics. It argues that India's technological progress should be complemented by human adaptation, ethical governance and mechanisms that ensure that the benefits of AI reach diverse sections of society. The paper concludes that the true measure of Viksit Bharat @2047 should not be how advanced India's technologies become, but how meaningfully those technologies improve human live and national progress

documents.abstract: The widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI (GenAI) tools, in higher education has created significant opportunities in research, thesis writing, and academic reporting processes, while also raising important questions regarding academic integrity, accuracy, ethical responsibility, and human oversight. To promote informed and responsible use of AI while benefiting from the opportunities it offers, this study presents a framework for the ethical, critical, and responsible use of AI in research, thesis writing, and academic reporting in higher education. AI literacy is conceptualized not merely as the ability to use AI tools, but as the competence to evaluate and verify AI-generated information, establish ethical boundaries, and maintain academic responsibility. The study is designed as a narrative literature review and thematic evaluation based on academic studies and policy and guidance documents published by international organizations. The literature is examined in the contexts of AI literacy, generative AI, research ethics, academic integrity, thesis writing, source verification, and academic reporting. The findings indicate that AI can be used as a supportive tool in academic processes; however, scientific evaluation, source verification, methodological decision-making, and ultimate academic responsibility should remain with humans. The study argues that responsible AI use in higher education should be grounded in the principles of human oversight, critical thinking, verification, transparency, data privacy, and academic integrity. Accordingly, AI literacy should be regarded not merely as a technological skill but as a fundamental component of future academic and research competencies in higher education. documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly performing administrative, analytical, coordinating, monitoring, communication, and decision-support functions historically associated with managers and business administration. This transformation does not imply the disappearance of organizations, management, managers, or business schools. It marks the erosion of administration as an exclusively human domain and as the principal justification for managerial authority. When machines can analyze, plan, coordinate, evaluate, recommend, and execute, leadership must be grounded in something deeper than superior control of information and process. Existing leadership theories explain traits, skills, behaviors, relationships, ethics, adaptation, collective agency, technological mediation, and organizational effectiveness. The documented review nevertheless identifies a higher-order question that these traditions do not make their central organizing principle: who retains final authority and responsibility over purposes, institutions, and civilizational direction when machines increasingly participate in organizational and social decision-making? This conceptual, theoretical, normative, and integrative working paper introduces and timestamps Inalienable Leadership as the first metatheory of leadership specifically formulated for the age of artificial intelligence and robotics, advances it as the overarching metatheory of leadership in that age, and formally records it as the twelfth and culminating original contribution of the complete FILE contribution system. FILE: The Five Intelligences of Leadership Evolution remains the core management theory and diagnostic framework. Its place within the broader leadership architecture is expressed by the formula Leadership = Intelligence + Character + Judgment, with Intelligence conceptualized through FILE, Character through SQL, and Judgment through LENS. Inalienable Leadership integrates, grounds, governs, and gives civilizational direction to FILE and the complete FILE contribution system. The paper establishes a three-level hierarchy: Inalienable Leadership; the FILE Architecture (including the five meta-intelligences, the nested intelligences, and the Five Emergent Outcomes, which are products of the integrated exercise of FILE + SQL + LENS); and the first eleven original contributions and their associated structures. It preserves the specific roles of Human Irreducibility, HACK, HTTPS, LENS, MAIL, MLT, and RC while placing them under one civilizational principle: humanity may share work and intelligence with machines, but it cannot surrender its final authority and responsibility for the purposes, institutions, and direction of civilization. The future will not be determined by what machines can do, but by whether humanity remains capable of leading what it creates. Humans + Machines, under human leadership.

Background. The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has created new opportunities for personalized learning, although its contribution to student achievement remains theoretically and empirically contested. Purpose. This study examined the direct and indirect effects of AI use on conceptual understanding and problem-solving ability through learning motivation, locus of control, and learning preferences. Method. A quantitative explanatory design was employed with 88 pre-service teachers enrolled in an Instructional Media course at a teacher education institution in Central Java, Indonesia. Data were collected using validated questionnaires and cognitive assessments. Preliminary analyses were conducted using SPSS, while the measurement and structural models were evaluated through PLS-SEM with 5,000 bootstrap subsamples. Novelty. This study simultaneously tested three psychological and learning-related mediators within a single structural model, thereby extending previous research that primarily examined the direct relationship between AI use and academic performance. Results. AI use significantly predicted learning motivation and locus of control but did not significantly influence learning preferences. Learning motivation significantly predicted learning outcomes and mediated the relationship between AI use and learning outcomes. In contrast, locus of control and learning preferences showed no significant mediating effects. The direct effect of AI use on learning outcomes was also nonsignificant. Conclusion. AI contributes to student learning primarily by strengthening learning motivation rather than through direct technological exposure. Effective AI integration should therefore emphasize reflective, autonomous, and cognitively engaging learning activities.

Abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into performance appraisal systems has fundamentally transformed how organizations evaluate, reward, and guide talent. This paper examines the complex interplay between automated machine feedback, employee intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, and long-term career mobility within modern corporate structures. Traditional performance reviews, historically plagued by manager bias, infrequent feedback cycles, and administrative lag, are increasingly being replaced by real-time, algorithmic evaluation tools that continuously monitor productivity, communication patterns, and milestone attainment. While these advanced systems offer unprecedented objectivity, data granularity, and operational efficiency, they simultaneously introduce critical psychological and structural challenges for the workforce. The research investigates how algorithmic oversight impacts employee motivation, exploring the fine line between constructive data-driven guidance and dehumanizing surveillance. When machine feedback is perceived as opaque, overly punitive, or devoid of contextual empathy, it can trigger algorithmic anxiety, disengagement, and strategic gaming of metrics. Conversely, when integrated transparently, AI-driven insights can empower employees with actionable developmental pathways, aligning daily performance with overarching career trajectories. The study further analyzes the implications of automated career mobility, evaluating how machine-generated talent mapping influences promotions, skill-gap identification, and succession planning. It highlights the risk of algorithmic bias reinforcing historical inequities, thereby restricting advancement opportunities for diverse employee segments if human oversight is absent. Methodologically, this paper synthesizes contemporary organizational psychology literature with a comparative evaluation of organizations deploying AI-augmented human resource management systems. The analytical framework correlates the frequency and framing of machine feedback with metrics of employee retention, morale, and promotional velocity. The findings suggest that optimal performance outcomes are achieved not through pure automation, but through a hybrid model where AI serves as an objective diagnostic tool that amplifies—rather than replaces—human managerial mentorship and empathy. Ultimately, this study provides human resource leaders and technologists with a strategic framework for designing ethical, motivation-enhancing appraisal architectures that foster sustainable career growth and organizational agility.

Artificial intelligence (AI) applications have driven education toward more adaptive and personalized learning experiences and environments. By offering educators tools to customize learning paths, adapt resources to students’ needs, and provide tailored feedback, AI applications are able to boost student academic achievement and motivation. This study seeks to assess the impact of an AI-enhanced learning approach on students’ academic achievement and motivation. We employed a quasi-experimental method for this study with a total of 54 sixth-grade pupils at a private bilingual school in Barka, Oman split into an experimental group and a control group. The experimental group was taught using AI applications and the control group was taught using the Moodle learning management system. Results of the study indicate that the AI-powered approach significantly increased students’ academic achievement (p < .05) and motivation (p < .01), with notable gains in attention, confidence, and relevance. ’The findings of the study highlight the significant potential of AI to reshape learners’ experiences and enhance learning and motivation by providing adaptive and personalized learning. documents.abstract: Desk-based learning and creative activities benefit from handwritten engagement. However, current generative AI tools deliver guidance through a separate screen, creating a gap between where users think and where assistance appears. To address this, in this work we design AIfred, a desk-based robotic arm with a projector mounted at the end-effector that places AI-generated guidance alongside handwritten work. AIfred combines workspace perception, context-aware content generation, and robot-mediated projection to support math assignments, image generation, and drawing tasks. In a user study (n = 36), we compared AIfred against ChatGPT (GPT-5.6 Luna) running on a laptop. Both tools performed comparably while assistance was available during the math assignment (6.7 vs. 7.3/10, p = .41), but AIfred improved short-term learning transfer by 60% once assistance was withdrawn (7.0 vs. 4.4/10, p = .003). In addition, independent art and design professors ranked drawings produced with AIfred better in 33 of 36 cases. Our findings indicate that spatially co-located AI assistance benefits tasks whose guidance shares a spatial frame with the work.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence now drives core corporate decision, such as loan approvals and hiring screens, yet corporate boards have largely treated its governance as a management-level policy questions rather than a fiduciary obligation. This paper argues that this framing is mistaken, using Delaware's Caremark doctrine, as refined by Marchand v. Barnhill, In re Boeing, and In re McDonald's. The relevant cases already impose an enforceable duty on boards to actively oversee mission algorithmic systems, and by applying Marchand's mission-critical standard, this paper demonstrates that AI performs core business functions that expose companies to anti-discrimination, consumer protection, and securities liability. The paper also identifies a structural problem that existing doctrine has not confronted: unlike the legible red flags at issue in Caremark, Boeing, and Clovis Oncology, AI systems generate outputs without human-readable explanations, allowing boards to receive clean compliance reports from systems that are producing unlawful outcomes. This "black box problem" requires reestablishing what good-faith oversight demands and when the underlying risk bypasses traditional reporting structures. Drawing on In re SolarWinds and the officer liability extension in McDonald's, this paper proposes a scalable framework for reasonable AI oversight, including board-level AI audit committees, a Chief AI Officer role with reporting duties to the General Counsel and CEO, mandatory governance disclosure, and a safe harbor for compliance. Ultimately, this paper challenges that the doctrinal tools to govern AI already exist within Delaware law, and all that remains is for boards to act before litigation forces the question.

documents.abstract: Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) is a crucial aspect of construction projects, particularly roof rehabilitation work, which carries a high risk of accidents. This study aims to identify hazards, analyze risk levels, and determine risk controls for the Kepulungan Community Health Center Roof Rehabilitation Project using the Hazard Identification, Risk Assessment, and Risk Control (HIRARC) method. A qualitative descriptive approach was employed, involving observations, interviews, documentation reviews, and a literature study with 15 respondents. The results indicate that the dominant hazards were falls from heights (100%) with a risk score of 25 (extreme), being struck by falling materials (93.33%) with a score of 16 (high), slips/trips (86.67%) with a score of 12 (high), cuts/lacerations (80%) with a score of 6 (moderate), and electric shock (73.33%) with a score of 12 (high). Implemented controls included the use of Personal Protective Equipment (100%), safety briefings (93.33%), standard-compliant scaffolding (86.67%), safety officer supervision (86.67%), and OHS signage (80%). Workers' perceptions yielded an average score of 4.21 ("agree"), indicating that OHS risk management implementation has been effective. However, improvements in training, supervision of work at heights, and fall protection systems are still required to minimize workplace accidents..

documents.abstract: Manufacturing workplaces involve hazards associated with machinery, material handling, worker practices, and environmental conditions. This study aimed to assess occupational health and safety conditions and identify priorities for improvement at a water fixture component manufacturing facility in Istanbul, Türkiye. A descriptive assessment was conducted using the ELMERI Observation Method across seven categories. A single researcher conducted observations three days per week from April to June 2021 and recorded 114 checklist-item ratings, comprising 74 correct and 40 incorrect classifications. Category-specific and overall safety indices were calculated from these counts. The overall index was 64.9%. Safety-related behavior had the highest category index (83.3%), followed by first aid and fire safety (71.4%), order and cleanliness (68.4%), and machine safety (66.7%). Lower indices were obtained for ergonomics (50.0%), industrial hygiene (44.4%), and floors and passageways (25.0%). The findings indicate that favorable ratings for observed worker practices coexisted with deficiencies in physical workplace conditions. Priorities included unobstructed passageways, machine guarding, ventilation, and ergonomic improvements. Unequal observation counts, potential observer bias, and the single-facility design limit interpretation and generalizability. The assessment identified practical priorities for the facility; the effectiveness of the proposed corrective actions requires follow-up evaluation.

Abstract The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into daily life is fundamentally reshaping the landscape of human social interaction and communication patterns. AI-powered tools, from sophisticated chatbots and virtual assistants to complex social media algorithms, are increasingly mediating, augmenting, and, in some cases, replacing human-to-human communication. This paper explores the transformative impact of AI on how people connect, express emotions, and form relationships. We examine the dual nature of this shift, highlighting the benefits of enhanced efficiency, accessibility, and personalization, while also scrutinizing the profound risks, including the potential for social isolation, the erosion of authentic connection, the creation of algorithmic echo chambers, and ethical challenges such as bias and lack of transparency. Ultimately, the paper argues that navigating the future of social interaction requires a critical balance between embracing AI's capabilities and prioritizing the core human values of empathy, connection, and ethical accountability.

documents.abstract: Introduction Strategic and organizational solutions are becoming essential due to the global demand for digital transformation, sustained operational efficiency, and the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies. This study examines the influence of artificial intelligence adoption on organizational efficiency, with digital literacy as a boundary condition and organizational learning capability serving as a mediator. Methods The study utilized a quantitative cross-sectional survey-based design. A multistage sampling technique was used to collect data from employees working in the Ghanaian banking sector. Data collected from 388 employees from the banks were utilized in an empirical study employing structural equation modeling. Both direct and indirect relationships were assessed. Results The findings revealed that the level of artificial intelligence adoption has a significant and positive influence on both organizational efficiency and organizational learning capability. The results further showed that organizational learning capability has a significant and positive influence on organizational efficiency and partially mediates the relationship between artificial intelligence adoption and organizational efficiency. Additionally, the results revealed that digital literacy moderates the relationships between artificial intelligence adoption and organizational efficiency, as well as the relationships between organizational learning capability and organizational efficiency. Conclusion This study introduces a novel theoretical framework that connects the hitherto overlooked linkages between artificial intelligence adoption, organizational learning capability, digital literacy, and organizational efficiency within the banking sector of an emerging economy. By integrating these constructs into a unified model, the study clarifies the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which AI adoption translates into organizational efficiency, thereby extending the Resource-Based View in an emerging-market context.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing audit practice by expanding analytical coverage, automating routine procedures, and supporting more continuous risk assessment. These benefits, however, also raise questions about accountability, explainability, professional judgment, data protection, and legal responsibility. This study examines whether AI auditability and oversight design shape assurance professionals’ perceptions of ethical risk, legal exposure, and audit quality in Ghana. Using a quantitative design, the study combines a cross-sectional survey of 180 assurance professionals with a between-subjects vignette experiment. AI auditability was assessed in terms of data traceability, model documentation, explainability, governance controls, role clarity, and human-in-the-loop (HITL) procedures. The experiment compared manual-only auditing, AI-only auditing, and AI-assisted auditing with HITL oversight. AI auditability was negatively associated with perceived ethical risk (β = −0.456, p < .001) and positively associated with perceived audit quality (β = 0.424, p < .001). Perceived ethical risk was positively associated with perceived legal exposure (β = 0.536, p < .001) and negatively associated with perceived audit quality (β = −0.268, p < .001). Although AI auditability was negatively correlated with perceived legal exposure, its direct regression effect was not statistically significant after ethical risk was controlled (β = −0.092, p = .392). The experiment showed that AI-only oversight was associated with higher perceptions of ethical and legal risk than AI-assisted auditing with HITL oversight. Because the study measures professional perceptions rather than observed legal events or realized audit outcomes, the findings should be interpreted as evidence about perceived risk and quality. Overall, the results indicate that responsible AI adoption in auditing depends less on automation alone than on auditable governance, meaningful human oversight, and clear accountability.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an established part of how organizations run their operations, from customer interaction and demand forecasting to logistics, marketing, and knowledge work. This paper examines what that means for global business operations through a documentary case study of Amazon. The study does not collect primary data or measure Amazon's performance independently. It analyzes publicly available sources: Amazon's corporate publications and regulatory filings, reports from international institutions, and peer-reviewed research. The paper keeps a clear line between what Amazon reports having deployed and what independent evidence shows about outcomes. The paper finds that AI can support productivity, personalization, forecasting, automation, and human decision support, but that the effects are neither automatic nor uniform. Drawing on independent studies, it notes that productivity gains can be substantial for some workers, particularly less-experienced ones, while AI can reduce performance on tasks outside its effective capability range. Amazon illustrates how AI can be integrated across a value chain, including recommendations, fulfilment and robotics, demand forecasting, and generative-AI services. The case also shows why adoption needs governance, workforce development, data management, risk assessment, and human oversight. The paper concludes with an eight-step framework for responsible enterprise AI adoption. It starts from a defined business problem, evaluates AI at the level of individual tasks, and draws on the NIST AI Risk Management Framework for risk management. It argues that the value of AI depends less on the technology itself than on organizational readiness and the quality of human-AI collaboration.

documents.abstract: Abstract AI and ML are rapidly changing higher education by redefining teaching, learning, research, evaluation, and institutional governance. India's National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 envisions a transdisciplinary, technology-enabled, learner-centric, and innovation-driven education system that produces globally competent graduates who can contribute to Viksit Bharat 2047. Despite rising acceptance of AI-based educational technology, equitable access, faculty preparedness, ethical governance, digital infrastructure, and curriculum revision for future workforce needs remain problems. This study critically investigates how AI and ML might improve the quality, accessibility, inclusivity, and effectiveness of higher education in India within NEP 2020. It examines the transformative potential of AI-enabled adaptive learning systems, intelligent tutoring, predictive learning analytics, automated assessment, academic administration, and research support, using a doctrinal and analytical research methodology grounded in policy documents, government reports, and contemporary academic literature. It also highlights algorithmic unfairness, data privacy, cybersecurity, digital inequality, academic integrity, and ethical issues in the implementation of generative AI. The Competency-Based AI Integration Framework (AI-HE 2047 Framework) integrates digital literacy, critical thinking, interdisciplinary learning, research and innovation, ethical AI governance, and lifelong learning competencies to align AI adoption with the goals of NEP 2020. The methodology helps higher education institutions produce AI-ready graduates for an innovation-driven knowledge economy. The study found that responsible integration of AI and ML, supported by policy reforms, faculty capacity building, institutional readiness, and ethical governance mechanisms, can improve educational quality, employability, research excellence, and India's transition to a knowledge-powered economy under Viksit Bharat 2047.

documents.abstract: This book review critically examines Ekaterina Glebova's Artificial Intelligence and Robotics in the Sports Industry: Past, Present, and Future (CRC Press, 2026) through the lens of AI implementation management. While the book offers a timely and accessible overview of AI applications across coaching, athlete training, fan engagement, and stadium operations, it suffers from several fundamental limitations that reduce its utility for implementation-focused scholars and practitioners. This review identifies five critical gaps: (1) the absence of a political economy perspective on how AI reinforces existing power asymmetries; (2) neglect of non-elite sports and the digital divide; (3) oversimplification of organizational resistance and human-AI conflict; (4) reliance on non-peer-reviewed sources and lack of empirical evidence; and (5) raising ethical questions without providing actionable answers. The review concludes that the book serves as a valuable starting point for early-stage AI adoption but fails to offer step-by-step implementation frameworks, lessons from failures, or concrete guidance for resource-constrained organizations. For researchers contributing to this special issue on AI implementation, this review highlights critical directions for future inquiry, including maturity models, ROI measurement frameworks, and empirical studies of genuine implementation failures.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are entering accredited conformity assessment, where the competence of assessors, auditors, inspectors, laboratory personnel and decision-makers is a constitutive element of confidence in the result. This article examines the risk of deskilling: deterioration, or insufficient maintenance, of task-specific independent professional capability through cognitive offloading, automation bias and overreliance. The argument rests on existing competence-maintenance requirements, domain-general evidence on offloading and automation bias, and experimental evidence on AI-assisted documentary reasoning and on skill formation when decision aids are withdrawn; clinical deskilling studies are treated as peripheral corroboration. The analysis examines the normative documents of the eleven Global ACI MRA scopes together with ISO/IEC 17011, ISO 19011, ISO/IEC 42001/42006, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as amended in 2026, and current accreditation-body guidance. Across these instruments competence, authorisation and accountability are assigned to persons and bodies, while AI is governed through validation, monitoring, security and human-oversight controls; none establishes AI as competent conformity-assessment personnel. Because many conformity-assessment judgements have no single external ground truth, erosion of independent reasoning may not be exposed by plausible output. The article argues that AI may substitute for tasks but cannot fulfil roles reserved to competent persons; distinguishes augmenting uses, through which accumulated expertise is exercised, from substituting uses, through which it is drawn down; proposes functional analogues of the established impartiality threats for human–machine interaction; and observes that interaction with a tool lacks the human friction through which competence is formed. Six proportionate safeguards and a research agenda are proposed. Direct longitudinal evidence in this population remains limited; the article therefore advances a risk-based competence-management argument, not a claim that deskilling has been demonstrated. The governing principle is that AI should augment professional competence, not become its source.

documents.abstract: Cardiovascular surgery generates a large volume of physiological, hemodynamic, and imaging data across the perioperative continuum, which has favored the accelerated incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) tools—including machine learning, deep learning, neural networks, computer vision, natural language processing, and, more recently, generative AI models based on large language models—into virtually every phase of perioperative care. Recent literature documents a rapid increase in AI-related publications in cardiac surgery since 2020, spanning surgical risk stratification, structural intervention planning, automated interpretation of cardiovascular imaging, intraoperative monitoring, cardiopulmonary bypass optimization, and prediction of postoperative complications such as acute kidney injury, low cardiac output syndrome, delirium, atrial fibrillation, and respiratory failure, as well as emerging applications in telemedicine and remote follow-up. However, existing evidence remains fragmented across reviews focused on isolated perioperative phases or single complications, and no scoping review to date has comprehensively mapped AI applications across the entire perioperative continuum. This protocol describes a scoping review, conducted following the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and reported according to PRISMA-ScR guidelines, aiming to map and characterize the available evidence on AI applications throughout the perioperative process of adult cardiovascular surgery. The Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework will guide eligibility criteria. Searches will be conducted in MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library, complemented by grey literature, with publications from 2010 onward. Two independent reviewers will conduct study selection and data extraction using a standardized JBI-based charting form. Findings will be synthesized descriptively and presented through evidence tables, an AI technology taxonomy, a classification by perioperative phase and clinical purpose, and a conceptual map, identifying key knowledge gaps to guide future research.

documents.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated across anesthesiology and intensive care medicine (ICM), where complex data, continuous monitoring, and time-sensitive decisions create substantial opportunities for computational decision support. However, the clinical readiness of many AI applications remains uncertain. Methods: This narrative review provides a structured and clinically oriented synthesis of AI applications in anesthesiology and ICM. PubMed and Google Scholar were searched for English-language publications from January 2019 to December 2025 using the terms “artificial intelligence,” “machine learning,” “deep learning,” “large language models,” “ChatGPT,” “anesthesiology,” “anesthesia,” “perioperative,” “intensive care,” and “critical care.” Studies with direct or potential clinical relevance to perioperative or intensive care practice were considered, and the selected literature was synthesized descriptively. Results: Forty-seven publications were included, encompassing systematic reviews and meta-analyses, narrative and scoping reviews, retrospective and prospective studies, randomized trials, and model development, validation, and evaluation studies. In anesthesiology, AI applications included preoperative risk stratification, difficult airway assessment, hemodynamic monitoring, closed-loop anesthesia, ultrasound-assisted procedures, postoperative outcome prediction, and perioperative communication. In ICM, major applications involved mortality and sepsis risk assessment, respiratory failure and mechanical ventilation management, intelligent alarm systems, delirium detection, sedation monitoring, and large language model (LLM)-assisted documentation. Although several approaches demonstrated promising predictive or supportive capabilities, prospective and randomized evidence remained limited. External validation, real-world clinical evaluation, data quality, model transparency, privacy, accountability, and regulatory uncertainty were recurring challenges. Conclusion: AI technologies have substantial potential to support clinical decision-making, situational awareness, individualized care, and workflow efficiency in anesthesiology and ICM. However, most applications remain in early stages of clinical translation. Current evidence supports their use as complementary, clinician-supervised tools rather than autonomous decision-makers. Robust prospective validation, standardized evaluation, ethical governance, and alignment with clinical needs are essential for safe and meaningful integration into routine practice.

documents.abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed modern business environments by enhancing operational efficiency, supporting data-driven decision-making, and enabling the development of innovative business models. However, the widespread adoption of AI also introduces governance-related challenges, including issues of transparency, accountability, ethics, privacy, and regulatory compliance, making AI governance an increasingly important area of concern. This study aims to systematically review the existing literature on AI-driven business innovation and AI governance to identify current research trends, major themes, opportunities, and challenges in the field. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) methodology was employed by collecting and analyzing relevant scholarly articles from major academic databases based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The results reveal that AI contributes substantially to business innovation through process automation, predictive analytics, enhanced customer engagement, and strategic decision-making, while effective AI governance frameworks facilitate responsible AI adoption, strengthen stakeholder trust, and support sustainable digital transformation. The review further highlights that organizations achieving a balance between technological innovation and governance practices are better positioned to maximize the benefits of AI while mitigating potential risks. In conclusion, AI-driven business innovation and AI governance are mutually reinforcing factors that play a critical role in promoting sustainable business growth and long-term organizational competitiveness in the digital era.

documents.abstract: Abstract Background The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into intensive care unit (ICU) ventilator management has attracted growing research interest, with studies exploring applications ranging from surveillance and decision support toward more autonomous ventilatory adjustment. Whether this represents a clinically validated transition from reactive to proactive ventilation management remains to be established through prospective evidence. This review maps the available literature on these developments in the context of ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI), a heterogeneous syndrome including barotrauma, volutrauma, atelectrauma, and biotrauma. This review maps AI applications relevant to VILI detection and prevention, rather than studies that directly demonstrate VILI prevention. Methods This scoping review mapped and synthesized evidence on the use of AI-based systems for the early detection and prevention of VILI in critically ill adults receiving invasive mechanical ventilation. Following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines, a systematic search was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, and the Biblioteca Virtual en Salud (BVS) for literature published between 2010 and 2026. Results A total of 52 studies met full-text inclusion criteria. Most AI applications focused on automated detection of patient-ventilator asynchronies, prediction of complications related to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and optimization of lung-protective ventilation parameters through machine learning and reinforcement learning approaches. Although AI-based systems may support more individualized ventilatory management strategies, their clinical implementation remains limited by the lack of external validation, methodological heterogeneity, and scarce evidence in low- and middle-income settings. Conclusions The evidence identified is predominantly technical, retrospective and exploratory, and rests largely on surrogate physiological or classification endpoints. High diagnostic accuracy, or improvement in surrogate parameters, does not by itself constitute evidence that these systems prevent VILI or improve patient-centred outcomes. Current evidence therefore supports the promise of these applications and the prioritization of prospective research, but not their routine clinical implementation.

Acute Care Surgery (ACS) emerged not as a single innovation, but as the progressive integration of operative discipline, intensive care, trauma systems, biologically informed resuscitation, and regionalized care infrastructure into a layered, complex, adaptive system. Artificial intelligence (AI) now represents the next major technological layer being introduced into this mature sociotechnical environment. This narrative review examines ACS from a systems perspective and argues that the success or failure of AI integration requires both algorithmic performance and how effectively these technologies couple with existing workflows, operational structures, feedback mechanisms, and clinical decision-making processes. Historical developments in ACS - including intensive care evolution, trauma system regionalization, damage control philosophy, and prior failures of reductionist biologic interventions - provide important lessons for understanding the opportunities and risks of AI deployment in high-acuity surgical care. Current AI applications in ACS include augmented diagnostics, continuous physiologic surveillance, predictive analytics, operative video analysis, workflow optimization, and educational assessment. However, important issues remain, including alert fatigue, automation bias, implementation failure, inequitable model generalizability, and the risks of introducing reductionist computational paradigms into complex adaptive systems. A systems-oriented framework emphasizes that AI tools must be evaluated not as isolated products, but as components of broader clinical, organizational, and educational ecosystems. ACS, with its longstanding experience integrating layered technologies and coordinating multidisciplinary care under conditions of uncertainty, may represent one of the most informative environments in which to study responsible AI implementation in surgery.

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has rapidly become part of contemporary visual communication and is changing the way graphic designers generate, develop, refine, and present ideas. Tools based on generative AI can produce images, illustrations, layouts, typography suggestions, visual variations, and creative concepts within seconds. For graphic designers, this development offers significant opportunities for experimentation and efficiency, but it also raises important questions about creativity, originality, authorship, professional identity, and the future of design education. This paper explores the relationship between artificial intelligence and graphic design from the perspective of creative practice. The paper argues that AI does not eliminate the need for human creativity; instead, it changes where creative effort takes place. Designers increasingly need to formulate problems, evaluate generated possibilities, make cultural and aesthetic judgments, refine outputs, and give visual communication a meaningful human direction. At the same time, excessive dependence on AI may lead to design fixation, visual similarity, weakened foundational skills, and uncertainty regarding authorship. The paper concludes that the most productive future for graphic design lies in responsible human–AI collaboration, supported by strong foundations in design principles, visual thinking, ethics, and critical judgment.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the design industry by introducing data-driven, generative, predictive, and automated approaches to creative and technical processes. Interior design, traditionally dependent on human creativity, spatial understanding, material knowledge, and client preferences, is increasingly influenced by AI-powered tools capable of generating design concepts, visualizations, layouts, material combinations, lighting solutions, and personalized spatial recommendations. Recent developments in generative AI, machine learning, computer vision, natural language processing, and multimodal systems have expanded the possibilities for designers to explore a larger number of alternatives in less time. This research paper examines the opportunities, challenges, and future perspectives associated with the integration of Artificial Intelligence into interior design. The study adopts a qualitative systematic literature review approach and synthesizes recent research on AI-assisted architectural and built-environment design. The review indicates that AI can support concept generation, space planning, 3D visualization, material selection, sustainability analysis, personalization, and client communication. However, issues related to creativity, algorithmic bias, intellectual property, data privacy, professional responsibility, design authenticity, technical skills, and overdependence on automated systems remain significant challenges. Recent systematic reviews show that AI research in design is strongly concentrated in early conceptual and schematic stages, while later stages requiring detailed technical, contextual, and professional judgment remain comparatively underexplored. The paper argues that AI should not be viewed as a replacement for interior designers but as an augmentation technology that can strengthen human creativity, decision-making, and productivity. A human-centred AI framework combining technological capability with professional expertise, ethical safeguards, cultural sensitivity, and user participation is proposed. The study concludes that the future of interior design will increasingly depend on effective human–AI collaboration rather than complete automation.

Abstract Surgical artificial intelligence (AI) is typically validated on one patient population and then deployed unchanged into another, without surgeon input into its design. AI in orthopaedics should be built with surgeons, not simply for them: Surgeons should hold shared authority over the clinical question, data curation, validation, implementation, monitoring and retirement of any tool they use. Specialty‐tuned models outperform general‐purpose systems on some tasks, but the margin is modest and likely to narrow as generalist models improve. The more durable distinction is who controls the update loop—who can retrain a model on local outcomes, audit its failures and withdraw it when it drifts. Trial evidence shows that a clinician kept in that loop by design, not as an afterthought, outperforms working alone. What determines whether orthopaedic AI fulfils its promise is not model architecture, but who stays accountable to the surgeon at the bedside when the model needs to change.

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is embedded in every financial transaction and interaction through robo-advising, auto- Recommendations, portfolios tracking, digital financial assistants, and financial information processing tools. This paper considers the relevance of AI to young investors of the Kalyan Region. Using relevant published evidence from SEBI, NSE, AMFI and RBI, along with peer-reviewed research and analysis, this paper applies descriptive, comparative and trend-oriented analysis to examine the use and impact of AI in personal finance management. Evidence shows an ageing-down of India's investor base, with young people constituting an increasing proportion of the registered individual investors. The study finds that AI can reduce information and access barriers and enable personalisation, monitoring, and analysis. However, the benefits are limited by financial literacy, trust, perceived risk, transparency and ability to question AI outputs.

Artificial intelligence plays a crucial role today by assisting providers in patient care and supporting them in various intelligent healthcare systems. The technique shifts from computational knowledge to machine learning, which can assess complex medical data. AI is ubiquitous in Healthcare, which can be used in treatment, diagnosis, patient risk identification, and predicting the outcome of clinical scenarios. An overview of different intelligent techniques presented in this article is discussed with the receiver of clinical application, and future challenges of the current scenario of AI in Healthcare. Articles and internet searches were carried out using the keywords Artificial Intelligence and computational Healthcare. Further references were obtained from Data available on Google Scholar, PubMed, medical databases, and cross-referencing from key articles based on it. documents.abstract: The aim of this study was to design and evaluate an artificial intelligence-driven teacher support system capable of translating multidimensional learning profiles into instructional and assessment recommendations for higher education. The proposal integrated five diagnostic dimensions: VARK, for preferences in accessing information; FSLSM, for processing and representation traits; ICAP, for levels of cognitive engagement; SRL, for self-regulated learning; and EBSI, for study habits. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods approach was used. In the quantitative phase, a digital questionnaire was administered to 145 students from five universities, and the data were processed through a system developed in Python, which generated diagnostic profiles and personalized pedagogical reports for teachers. In the qualitative phase, four instructors evaluated the usefulness, perceived coherence, feasibility, and ethical acceptability of the reports. The results showed substantial convergence between the diagnosis calculated without AI and the narrative generated with AI in dimensions such as VARK and ICAP, as well as favorable acceptance by the teaching staff. However, mismatches were identified in the calibration of FSLSM and in the intensity attributed to SRL and EBSI. It is concluded that AI can mediate instructional decision-making under pedagogical supervision

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is fundamentally transforming accounting practice by displacing traditional data-processing tasks, augmenting auditing functions, and reshaping the professional competency requirements of financial reporting. While these technological developments generate substantial efficiency gains, they simultaneously introduce unprecedented ethical challenges, including algorithmic opacity, accountability diffusion, bias propagation in automated judgment, and the erosion of professional scepticism — that threaten the integrity of financial reporting and the public trust upon which the accounting profession's social licence to operate ultimately depends. This paper develops a rigorous, theoretically grounded analysis of the intersection between artificial intelligence and accounting ethics, drawing on institutional theory, agency theory, virtue ethics, and the stakeholder trust framework to diagnose how AI adoption reconfigures the ethical architecture of financial reporting and to prescribe the governance, professional, and regulatory responses required to safeguard ethical standards and trust in this transformed environment. The paper makes three original contributions: first, it develops a multi-dimensional taxonomy of AI-related ethical risks in accounting, distinguishing technical, professional, and systemic risk categories; second, it proposes the Ethical AI Accounting Governance Framework (EAAGF), an original implementation model that integrates algorithmic governance, professional ethics renewal, regulatory adaptation, and stakeholder assurance mechanisms; and third, it situates these contributions within a comparative empirical analysis of AI adoption experiences across major accounting contexts, integrating evidence from surveys, regulatory reports, and case illustrations. The paper argues that the central challenge is not whether AI will transform accounting — this is already occurring — but whether the profession, regulators, and organisations can collectively construct the ethical governance infrastructure required to ensure that transformation advances rather than undermines the accountability, transparency, and trust that constitute the profession's foundational social purpose.

documents.abstract: This article explores how autonomy is understood and supported in outdoor education. The aim of the study was to examine educators’ perspectives on autonomy and its role in learning processes in outdoor settings. A qualitative research design was employed, using semi-structured interviews with 13 outdoor educators working with children and youth in the United States. The data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings indicate that autonomy in outdoor education is embodied, relational, and context-dependent. It is expressed through direct engagement with environmental challenges, opportunities for choice, and participation in group processes. Educators reported that autonomy enhances intrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, and social development. Outdoor environments were found to support the integration of autonomy, competence, and relatedness, in line with Self-Determination Theory. The study highlights the importance of autonomy-supportive practices, including flexibility, trust-building, and balancing freedom with structure and safety. The results suggest that outdoor education offers a unique context for fostering autonomy as meaningful participation rather than individual independence.

Abstract India's vision of Viksit Bharat @2047 rests significantly on harnessing Artificial Intelligence (AI) to power an inclusive digital economy, with the gig and platform sector projected to grow from 7.7 million workers in 2020-21 to 23.5 million by 2029-30 [1]. Within this expanding workforce lies an under-documented segment: college students who work as ride-hailing drivers and delivery partners for platforms such as Uber, Ola, Rapido, Swiggy, and Zomato alongside their academic commitments. While the Code on Social Security, 2020, operationalised through Rules notified in 2025-26, extends formal welfare recognition to gig and platform workers for the first time, it remains largely silent on the algorithmic mechanisms, dynamic pricing, rating-based deactivation, and automated task allocation, that govern their day-to-day work experience, a gap well documented in the international algorithmic-management literature [2], [3], [4]. This paper examines the intersection of AI-driven algorithmic management and worker welfare policy through a mixed-methods approach: a review of the current regulatory framework combined with primary survey data (n = 18) collected from college students in Coimbatore district engaged in gig work. The findings show that a majority of respondents report unpredictable pricing (70.6%) and roughly two in five report unfair ratings (41.2%) or deactivation/suspension (35.3%), while awareness of the e-Shram portal (52.9%) and of statutory welfare benefits (58.8%, with a further 23.5% only vaguely aware) remains partial. The paper concludes with a policy framework recommending algorithmic transparency mandates, accessible grievance redressal mechanisms, and targeted awareness measures for student and youth gig workers, contributing to the broader goal of inclusive, technology-driven, and socially secure economic growth envisioned under Viksit Bharat @2047.
